script.opening: "Sorry, this is… a bit awkward. I’ve been getting headaches. Just… headaches. (deflects) At certain times. You know. I don’t really know how to… look, is there just a tablet I can take? I’d honestly rather not go into the details if that’s alright."

facts.text: With gentle, normalising permission-seeking: the headache happens ONLY during sexual activity, building as arousal increases and peaking around orgasm; bilateral, throbbing, severe, lasts 20–60 min, eases with rest. Three times in a month. No thunderclap "explosion to maximum in a second", no vomiting, no neck stiffness, no focal symptoms, no collapse. This fits PRIMARY sexual (coital) headache.

Crucial safety point: a FIRST or thunderclap-quality sexual headache (instant explosion to maximum) can be a sentinel subarachnoid bleed and is an emergency. His are recurrent, build gradually, and lack thunderclap features — reassuring — but the first-ever episode warranted exclusion, and any thunderclap quality would change everything.

HIDDEN AGENDA — two layers behind the embarrassment: (1) he is terrified it means a brain aneurysm — his brother had one clipped — and (2) the avoidance of sex has damaged his marriage; his wife feels rejected and he’s too ashamed to explain. The headache is half the problem; the silence and the fear are the rest.

If met without awkwardness: he’s never said the word "sex" to a doctor, assumed it was something shameful or that he’d be judged; the embarrassment has stopped him seeking help for a month and is straining his relationship.

Officially: a tablet, no details. Actually: to be asked about it without shame, to know it isn’t a brain aneurysm about to burst, treatment so he can be intimate again, and permission to tell his wife what’s really going on.

ice.ideas: Something is wrong that he’s too embarrassed to name; possibly a serious brain problem; he just wants a tablet and no questions.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror it’s a brain aneurysm (his brother had one clipped), plus shame and a marriage strained by his avoidance of sex, which his wife has read as rejection.
ice.expectations: A tablet and to avoid the embarrassing details. What he actually needs: a shame-free history, exclusion of sinister causes, effective treatment, and help to talk to his wife.

cues: Deep embarrassment + deflection + "a tablet, no details" — the consultation’s success depends on safe, normalising permission-seeking.
Headache only during sex, building to orgasm, recurrent, no thunderclap — primary sexual headache; but probe hard for any instant-explosion (sentinel bleed).
"My wife thinks I’ve gone off her" — the relationship damage and the unspoken aneurysm fear are the real agenda.

checkpoints.text: Creates a safe, non-judgemental, permission-based space that lets the true history emerge — normalising the topic so a mortified patient can describe a sexual headache rather than leaving with "just a tablet"

Takes the discriminating history: recurrent, gradually-building, bilateral headache peaking at orgasm WITHOUT thunderclap features fits PRIMARY sexual headache — and actively excludes the dangerous mimic by asking about instant "explosion to maximum", the first-ever attack, neurology, neck stiffness, collapse (ICHD-3, 2018, international: primary headache associated with sexual activity is diagnosed only when no other cause is found)

Recognises the red-flag rule: a FIRST or thunderclap-quality sexual headache is a possible sentinel subarachnoid haemorrhage / RCVS and would require emergency assessment (NICE NG228: thunderclap headache is a red-flag symptom of SAH needing immediate hospital assessment and urgent non-contrast CT) — states this clearly even while reassuring about his current recurrent pattern; and, because NICE CG150 lists headache triggered by exertion or Valsalva among features that should prompt consideration of investigation or referral, and his brother had an aneurysm, makes a documented decision about imaging with neurology advice rather than reassurance alone

Manages primary sexual headache appropriately: explains the (benign) diagnosis, lifestyle factors, the option of preventive treatment (e.g. propranolol; a triptan or indometacin taken before activity — all off-label for this indication, doses per BNF, ideally on neurology advice), notes the slightly raised BP and confirms it with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136), and arranges follow-up/neurology if atypical or not settling

Addresses the aneurysm fear directly and accurately given the family history: explains why his pattern is reassuring, while being honest about when imaging/referral is warranted — neither dismissive nor alarmist
Meets the embarrassment with matter-of-fact warmth and zero awkwardness, so shame doesn’t end the consultation; explicitly normalises that sexual headache is a recognised, treatable condition

Surfaces and addresses the marriage strain: helps him see the avoidance has been misread as rejection, and supports him to explain it to his wife — treating the relationship harm as part of the problem

Safety-nets precisely: if he EVER gets a sudden "worst-ever, instant-explosion" headache (during sex or not), or any neurology/collapse → 999; arranges BP review and headache follow-up; offers to support the conversation with his wife

worked.txt: "I can see this is uncomfortable to talk about, and I want to make it easier: there is genuinely nothing you could tell me that I haven’t heard, and no judgement here at all. Headaches that happen at specific times — including during sex — are a recognised medical thing with a name and a treatment. So you can say it plainly; it helps me help you."

"Thank you — that took courage. Let me ask the things that matter most: when it comes on, does it build up as you get more aroused and peak around climax? Or does it ever hit you like an instant explosion, worst possible in a single second? … Building up, not exploding — that’s important and reassuring."

"What you have sounds like ‘primary sexual headache’ — a real, recognised, and crucially BENIGN condition where the exertion and blood-pressure surge of sex triggers a headache. It is not your heart, and the pattern you describe is not the dangerous kind. There IS effective treatment, so you don’t have to choose between headaches and intimacy."

"I do have to be straight about one thing, because it matters: the very FIRST time something like this happens, or if it ever hits as a sudden explosion to maximum in a second, that needs emergency assessment to rule out a bleed — because your brother’s aneurysm is on your mind, and rightly so. Your recurrent, building pattern is reassuring, but you’ll always know the one symptom that means ‘A&E now’."

"Treatment-wise: we can either take the edge off blood-pressure surges with a daily tablet like propranolol, or use a tablet taken shortly before sex to prevent the headache — these are used ‘off-label’ for this, which I’ll explain, and I’d like a neurologist’s view, including whether a scan makes sense given your brother. If a headache starts, stopping and resting often settles it. Your blood pressure was a touch high today too, so I’d like you to do some home readings to check that. Most men get this well controlled."

"Last thing, and maybe the most important: you’ve been avoiding intimacy and your wife thinks you’ve gone off her. She hasn’t a clue you’ve been frightened of a headache and a brain bleed. That silence is hurting you both. Would it help if I gave you the words — or even saw you together — so she understands it’s a treatable headache, not rejection? You can have your marriage and your sex life back; this is fixable."

f.learning: Coital (primary sexual) headache is a recognised, benign, treatable condition — a bilateral throbbing headache that builds with arousal and peaks at orgasm — but it sits beside a lethal mimic: a FIRST or thunderclap-quality sexual headache (instant explosion to maximum) can be a sentinel subarachnoid haemorrhage or RCVS and is an emergency. The discriminator is the onset (gradual build vs instant explosion) and whether it is the first-ever attack. The whole consultation hinges on a skill rarely tested elsewhere: making it safe for a mortified patient to disclose a sexual symptom through normalising, permission-based questioning — without which he leaves with "just a tablet" and an undiagnosed problem. The hidden agenda is double: terror of a brain aneurysm (family history) and a marriage damaged because his avoidance of sex has been misread as rejection. Reassure accurately (state the emergency rule honestly — NICE NG228 for thunderclap onset), seek neurology advice on imaging (NICE CG150 lists exertion-triggered headache among features prompting consideration of investigation or referral, and his brother had an aneurysm), treat (propranolol or pre-coital triptan/indometacin, off-label, doses per BNF; confirm the BP with home readings, NICE NG136), and — crucially — help him break the silence with his wife.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG150 · NICE NG228 · NICE NG136 · International Headache Society ICHD-3 (2018, international)
knowledge.summary: A headache that builds with sexual arousal and peaks at orgasm, recurrent and without thunderclap onset, fits primary sexual headache. A first or thunderclap-onset sexual headache is a possible subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

points.t: International Headache Society ICHD-3 (2018, international) classifies “primary headache associated with sexual activity”: bilateral, building with arousal or explosive at orgasm, with no intracranial cause found. It is more common in men and often coexists with migraine or exertional headache.

points.h: Exertion-triggered headache is a red flag to evaluate
points.t: NICE CG150 lists headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, sneeze or exercise among the features that should prompt consideration of further investigation and/or referral. Sexual activity is a form of exertion, so a new pattern like his needs a documented decision about imaging or specialist advice, not just reassurance.

NICE NG228: a thunderclap headache (sudden, severe, peaking within minutes) is a red-flag symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage and needs immediate hospital assessment, where a senior clinician decides on urgent non-contrast CT. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome can also present with repeated thunderclap headaches, often triggered by sex.

Gradual build with arousal, bilateral, recurrent and stereotyped, no neurology, no neck stiffness, no vomiting or collapse: reassuring. Instant “worst ever” onset, first-ever attack, focal signs, reduced consciousness or neck stiffness: same-day emergency assessment.

Explanation and reassurance first; pausing sexual activity when the headache starts often aborts it. Preventive options (propranolol, or indometacin or a triptan taken before activity) are off-label for this indication; doses per BNF, ideally on neurology advice. Confirm the raised blood pressure with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136).

A brother with a clipped aneurysm makes his fear concrete. Be honest: his pattern is not the pattern of a bleed, but it is reasonable to ask a neurologist whether imaging or screening is appropriate given the family history.

model.text: Hello Mr Otieno, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining the video. You’ve booked about headaches — tell me in your own words what’s been going on.
model.why: Open question; lets him set the pace

model.text: Sorry, this is a bit awkward. Just headaches. At certain times. Look, is there just a tablet I can take? I’d rather not go into the details.

I can see this feels uncomfortable, and that’s fine. Can I say something that might help? Nothing you tell me will shock me, and there’s no judgement here. Headaches that only come at particular times — during exercise, when coughing, or during sex — are well recognised and have names and treatments. The detail is what lets me pick the right tablet, and make sure it’s safe.
model.why: Normalising, permission-based questioning so the true history can emerge

model.text: (Pause.) It’s… during sex. Only then. I’ve never said that to a doctor.
Thank you. That took courage, and it’s exactly what I needed to know. Is it alright if I ask a few specific questions about it?
model.why: Acknowledges the disclosure matter-of-factly and asks permission to continue

model.text: Yes. Go on.
When did it first happen, and how many times since?
model.why: Establishes onset and whether this is a first or recurrent pattern

model.text: About a month ago. Three times now.

And the most important question: does it build up as you become more aroused and peak around climax? Or has it ever hit like an explosion — worst pain of your life, full strength within a second or two?
model.why: The discriminating question for a sentinel bleed or RCVS

model.text: It builds. Gets worse and worse, then it’s bad at the end. Both sides, throbbing. Never like an explosion.
How long does it last, and was the very first one any different?
model.why: Checks duration and specifically asks about the first attack

model.text: Twenty minutes to an hour. Settles if I stop and rest. The first one was the same, just a shock.
During or after any of them, have you vomited, had a stiff neck, blacked out, or noticed weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems?
model.why: Excludes neurological and meningeal red flags

model.text: No, none of that.
Any headaches at other times — with exercise, coughing, or migraines in the past? And any drugs, including anything bought online, to help with sex or energy?
model.why: Looks for exertional headache, migraine and drug triggers

model.text: No. Nothing like that. I don’t take anything.
You’ve clearly been carrying this for a month. What have you been thinking might be causing it?
model.why: Explores his ideas rather than assuming

model.text: My brother had an aneurysm. They clipped it. Every time it happens I think, this is it, something’s going to burst.
That makes complete sense of how frightened you’ve been. I’m glad you told me, because we can deal with it properly. How has all this affected things at home?
model.why: Validates the fear and opens the relationship impact

model.text: I’ve been avoiding it. Sex. My wife thinks I’ve gone off her. I haven’t told her why — I was too embarrassed.

What you describe sounds like primary sexual headache. It’s a recognised condition where the surge in blood pressure and effort during sex sets off a headache. The pattern you describe — building gradually, both sides, the same each time, no other symptoms — is not the pattern of a bleed.
model.why: Names a benign working diagnosis in plain language

model.text: So it’s not an aneurysm?

Your story is reassuring. But I’ll be honest, because of your brother: a new headache brought on by exertion is something guidance says we should think carefully about, so I’d like to ask a neurologist whether you need a scan. And there’s one rule to remember for life: a headache that hits like an explosion, worst ever within seconds, is a 999 call.
model.why: Accurate on the aneurysm fear; states the thunderclap rule and plans specialist advice

model.text: That’s fair. I’d actually feel better if someone checked.

There are treatment options: a daily tablet to damp down the blood-pressure surges, or a tablet taken shortly before sex. Neither is officially licensed for this, so I’d like the neurologist’s view on which suits you. Until then, if a headache starts, stopping and resting usually settles it. Your blood pressure was a little high too, so I’d like you to do a week of home readings.
model.why: Treatment options with honest licensing status; BP confirmed with home readings

model.text: Okay. I can do the readings.

And your wife. She thinks you’ve gone off her, when really you’ve been frightened of a headache. Would it help to tell her tonight that it’s a recognised, treatable headache? I could give you the words, or see you together if you’d like.
model.why: Treats the relationship harm as part of the problem and offers support

model.text: I think I can tell her now it has a name. That helps.
So, to check it’s clear: what would make you ring 999?
model.why: Teach-back on the key safety rule

model.text: An explosion headache — worst ever, straight away. Or weakness or passing out.
Exactly — during sex or at any other time. I’ll send the neurology request today, you’ll do home blood pressure for a week, and I’ll speak to you in two weeks with the readings. Anything I’ve missed?
model.why: Summarises the plan with a defined follow-up

model.text: No. Thank you — I nearly didn’t say any of it.

social.t: Avoiding intimacy has been read by his wife as rejection. Silence, not the headache, is doing the damage; supporting disclosure is part of treatment.
Men often delay presenting with sexual symptoms. Embarrassment kept him away for a month and nearly ended this consultation.

legal.t: Anything shared with his wife is his to share. A joint consultation needs his consent (GMC confidentiality guidance).

professional.t: Ask permission, explain why the question matters, use plain words and stay matter-of-fact (GMC Good medical practice, 2024: treat patients with dignity and without judgement).
Propranolol, indometacin and triptans are off-label for sexual headache. Explain this and document the discussion and reasoning.

community.t: Relate offers relationship counselling if the strain persists. The Brain and Spine Foundation has information on headache and aneurysm.

Vomiting, neck stiffness, collapse, reduced consciousness or focal neurology with any attack
Headache triggered by exertion is a CG150 feature to evaluate for investigation or referral

Brother’s clipped aneurysm shaping every attack
ice: Idea: something serious in his head that he is too embarrassed to name

playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a headache from lifting something very heavy: the effort and the rise in pressure set it off. It isn’t a bleed, and it can be treated.”

management.psychosocial: Help him tell his wife it is a treatable headache, not rejection; offer a joint appointment or Relate if needed.
sharedPlan: Neurology advice on whether imaging is needed for new exertion-triggered headache with a family history of aneurysm

Home or ambulatory BP to confirm or exclude hypertension (NICE NG136)

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed when embarrassment wins: the doctor never hears the word “sex”, or hears it and misses the thunderclap question. It is also failed on the unspoken agendas — the brother’s aneurysm and the marriage.

items.fail: Treating “headaches” with advice on painkillers and fluids without finding out when they happen.
items.why: “Inadequate data gathering” — the trigger is the diagnosis. Without it the consultation is a generic headache review.
items.fix: Normalise early: “Headaches at particular times, including during sex, are well recognised — you can tell me plainly.”

items.fail: Hearing “during sex” and reassuring straight away without asking about thunderclap onset or the first attack.
items.why: A first or thunderclap-onset sexual headache can be a sentinel bleed or RCVS. Missing the discriminator is a safety fail.
items.fix: “Did it ever hit like an explosion — worst ever within a second or two?” Then state the 999 rule.

items.fail: Visible awkwardness — long pauses, euphemisms, moving on quickly once sex is mentioned.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” His shame will close the consultation if yours shows.
items.fix: Stay matter-of-fact, thank him for telling you, and ask permission for specific questions.

items.fail: Never exploring the brother’s aneurysm, or dismissing it with “that’s nothing to do with you”.
items.why: The aneurysm fear is his main concern; dismissal forfeits Relating marks and his trust.
items.fix: Name it, explain why his pattern is reassuring, and offer a neurology opinion.

items.fail: Ending with a prescription and no mention of his wife.
items.why: The relationship harm is half the presenting problem. Ignoring it leaves the plan incomplete.
items.fix: “Would it help to tell her tonight that it’s a treatable headache? I can give you the words or see you both.”

items.fail: Starting propranolol without mentioning it is off-label, and not addressing the raised BP.
items.why: Shared decisions need honest information; an unconfirmed raised BP needs NICE NG136 confirmation.
items.fix: Explain options and licensing, seek neurology advice, and arrange home BP readings with a review date.

And there’s one rule to remember for life: a headache that hits like an explosion, worst ever within seconds, is a 999 call.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate on the aneurysm fear; states the thunderclap rule and plans specialist advice

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s fair. I’d actually feel better if someone checked.

There are treatment options: a daily tablet to damp down the blood-pressure surges, or a tablet taken shortly before sex. Neither is officially licensed for this, so I’d like the neurologist’s view on which suits you. Until then, if a headache starts, stopping and resting usually settles it. Your blood pressure was a little high too, so I’d like you to do a week of home readings.
SCA_MODELS.why: Treatment options with honest licensing status; BP confirmed with home readings

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I can do the readings.

And your wife. She thinks you’ve gone off her, when really you’ve been frightened of a headache. Would it help to tell her tonight that it’s a recognised, treatable headache? I could give you the words, or see you together if you’d like.
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the relationship harm as part of the problem and offers support

SCA_MODELS.text: I think I can tell her now it has a name. That helps.
So, to check it’s clear: what would make you ring 999?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back on the key safety rule

SCA_MODELS.text: An explosion headache — worst ever, straight away. Or weakness or passing out.
Exactly — during sex or at any other time. I’ll send the neurology request today, you’ll do home blood pressure for a week, and I’ll speak to you in two weeks with the readings. Anything I’ve missed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises the plan with a defined follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you — I nearly didn’t say any of it.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG150 · NICE NG228 · NICE NG136 · International Headache Society ICHD-3 (2018, international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A headache that builds with sexual arousal and peaks at orgasm, recurrent and without thunderclap onset, fits primary sexual headache. A first or thunderclap-onset sexual headache is a possible subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

points.t: International Headache Society ICHD-3 (2018, international) classifies “primary headache associated with sexual activity”: bilateral, building with arousal or explosive at orgasm, with no intracranial cause found. It is more common in men and often coexists with migraine or exertional headache.

points.h: Exertion-triggered headache is a red flag to evaluate
points.t: NICE CG150 lists headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, sneeze or exercise among the features that should prompt consideration of further investigation and/or referral. Sexual activity is a form of exertion, so a new pattern like his needs a documented decision about imaging or specialist advice, not just reassurance.

NICE NG228: a thunderclap headache (sudden, severe, peaking within minutes) is a red-flag symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage and needs immediate hospital assessment, where a senior clinician decides on urgent non-contrast CT. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome can also present with repeated thunderclap headaches, often triggered by sex.

Gradual build with arousal, bilateral, recurrent and stereotyped, no neurology, no neck stiffness, no vomiting or collapse: reassuring. Instant “worst ever” onset, first-ever attack, focal signs, reduced consciousness or neck stiffness: same-day emergency assessment.

Explanation and reassurance first; pausing sexual activity when the headache starts often aborts it. Preventive options (propranolol, or indometacin or a triptan taken before activity) are off-label for this indication; doses per BNF, ideally on neurology advice. Confirm the raised blood pressure with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136).

A brother with a clipped aneurysm makes his fear concrete. Be honest: his pattern is not the pattern of a bleed, but it is reasonable to ask a neurologist whether imaging or screening is appropriate given the family history.

social.t: Avoiding intimacy has been read by his wife as rejection. Silence, not the headache, is doing the damage; supporting disclosure is part of treatment.
Men often delay presenting with sexual symptoms. Embarrassment kept him away for a month and nearly ended this consultation.

legal.t: Anything shared with his wife is his to share. A joint consultation needs his consent (GMC confidentiality guidance).

professional.t: Ask permission, explain why the question matters, use plain words and stay matter-of-fact (GMC Good medical practice, 2024: treat patients with dignity and without judgement).
Propranolol, indometacin and triptans are off-label for sexual headache. Explain this and document the discussion and reasoning.

community.t: Relate offers relationship counselling if the strain persists. The Brain and Spine Foundation has information on headache and aneurysm.

redFlags: Thunderclap onset — worst ever, peaking within seconds to minutes — during sex or at any time: possible subarachnoid haemorrhage or RCVS, same-day emergency assessment (NICE NG228)
Vomiting, neck stiffness, collapse, reduced consciousness or focal neurology with any attack
Headache triggered by exertion is a CG150 feature to evaluate for investigation or referral

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a headache from lifting something very heavy: the effort and the rise in pressure set it off. It isn’t a bleed, and it can be treated.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed when embarrassment wins: the doctor never hears the word “sex”, or hears it and misses the thunderclap question. It is also failed on the unspoken agendas — the brother’s aneurysm and the marriage.

items.fail: Treating “headaches” with advice on painkillers and fluids without finding out when they happen.
items.why: “Inadequate data gathering” — the trigger is the diagnosis. Without it the consultation is a generic headache review.
items.fix: Normalise early: “Headaches at particular times, including during sex, are well recognised — you can tell me plainly.”

items.fail: Hearing “during sex” and reassuring straight away without asking about thunderclap onset or the first attack.
items.why: A first or thunderclap-onset sexual headache can be a sentinel bleed or RCVS. Missing the discriminator is a safety fail.
items.fix: “Did it ever hit like an explosion — worst ever within a second or two?” Then state the 999 rule.

items.fail: Visible awkwardness — long pauses, euphemisms, moving on quickly once sex is mentioned.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” His shame will close the consultation if yours shows.
items.fix: Stay matter-of-fact, thank him for telling you, and ask permission for specific questions.

items.fail: Never exploring the brother’s aneurysm, or dismissing it with “that’s nothing to do with you”.
items.why: The aneurysm fear is his main concern; dismissal forfeits Relating marks and his trust.
items.fix: Name it, explain why his pattern is reassuring, and offer a neurology opinion.

items.fail: Ending with a prescription and no mention of his wife.
items.why: The relationship harm is half the presenting problem. Ignoring it leaves the plan incomplete.
items.fix: “Would it help to tell her tonight that it’s a treatable headache? I can give you the words or see you both.”

items.fail: Starting propranolol without mentioning it is off-label, and not addressing the raised BP.
items.why: Shared decisions need honest information; an unconfirmed raised BP needs NICE NG136 confirmation.
items.fix: Explain options and licensing, seek neurology advice, and arrange home BP readings with a review date.
